01The shape of Gemma4 E4B

42 layers, hidden size 2560 — but the interesting structure is in which layers get which attention, and which layers own a KV cache at all.

The 5:1 iSWA rhythm. Five of every six layers attend through a sliding window (shuttered rows); every sixth layer is a full global-attention layer. The pattern is one line of config logic — (layer + 1) % sliding_window_pattern != 0 — with the pattern defaulting to 6 but overridden by model metadata (5 for E2B).

gpt.zig:360 · gpt.zig:234

Two head sizes. Global layers run head_dim 512; sliding layers run 256. Global attention has twice the per-head width, and the attention kernels carry both shapes (hd512 has its own generated flash-prefill variant).

gpt.zig:540

The tail shares earlier K/V. On Gemma4 E4B, 24 of 42 layers write K/V; the 18 tail layers skip the K/V projection entirely and read a donor layer's blocks. That's 18 layers without independent K/V computation; physical allocation savings depend on the storage route.

Implementation detail
Conceptual baseline

a conventional decoder computes independent K/V in each attention layer.

Antfly

Gemma E-series tail layers reuse donors of the same attention type.

gpt.zig:489

02Tokens in

Before any tensor exists, a string becomes ids and a request becomes a session.

The prompt is split by a SentencePiece tokenizer into pieces from a 262,144-entry vocabulary. Words can span several pieces; the split and ids shown here are illustrative, not the output of a tokenizer run. These chapters follow text decoding; multimodal inputs add projected image or audio features.

sentencepiece.zig:20

The HTTP handler hands the request to the session factory, which reads the model manifest and resolves it to ModelFamily.gemma — one tag in the unified GPT config. The generation pipeline and GPT architecture are shared with other decoder families, while Gemma-specific helpers and Metal lowerers implement PLE, shared KV, channel handling, and prepared decode paths.

03Embeddings, and then embeddings again (PLE)

Gemma-4 looks its tokens up twice: once for the hidden state, and once for a per-layer embedding lane that supplies a distinct learned input to each layer.

The ordinary part first: the token id selects one row of the embedding table and becomes a 2560-wide hidden state, multiplied by the configured embedding scale (Gemma uses √2560).

Then the second lookup. Gemma-4's per-layer embeddings (PLE) run a token lookup alongside a projection of the initial hidden state. The projection is normalized in 256-wide chunks and combined with the scaled token embeddings. The resulting vector is sliced across all 42 layers, each receiving its own gated slice. It's part of the model — skip it and you are running a different network.

gpt.zig:11135 · gpt.zig:159

PLE is not free. The per_layer_model_proj matvec has 10752×2560 weights. The qualified Metal path stages eligible dense slots to q8_0 at load time, default-on: about 55.1 MB in BF16 becomes 29.2 MB in Q8_0, a 25.8 MB weight-read reduction per matvec. These are tensor-size calculations, not measured memory traffic. Historical probes retained identical greedy token ids; quantization does not guarantee that for every prompt.

Implementation detail
Conceptual baseline

a conventional decoder embedding initializes the hidden state once.

Antfly

Gemma adds a per-layer input lane; its model projection can be quantized while preserving the architectural operation.

gpt.zig:11135

04Attention: windows, groups, and norms in the right places

One attention block, taken apart: Gemma-4 puts RMS norms on the Q and K heads themselves; eligible Metal routes fuse each head norm with its RoPE operation.

After the QKV projection, each query and key head is RMS-normalized per head — controlling the scale of attention logits. Antfly can lower each norm-plus-RoPE pair as a fused ⟨head_rms ⋄ rope⟩ dispatch. Q and K are separate calls; this is not one combined Q/K dispatch.

gpt.zig:6858 · metal_kernels.m:7616

Grouped-query attention. Gemma4 E4B runs 8 query heads against 2 KV heads — 4 queries share each K/V bank. Relative to eight distinct KV heads of the same width, that reduces KV elements by 4×. Its effect on total latency depends on context length, weight traffic, and the selected attention kernel.

The two masks. A sliding layer may only read a fixed trailing window of the sequence; every sixth layer can read the full causal history. The layer types also differ in head dimension and RoPE settings. Attention dispatch depends on those shapes, context length, and route policy.

gpt.zig:360

05The KV cache is a filing system

Drag the slider through a schematic of KV ownership and retention. The replay uses 16-token blocks and a shortened window; it is not a runtime allocation trace.

The general KV manager uses page_size_tokens = 16, and pages may pack several layers. This drawing separates logical layer groups to show which ones write K/V. It does not represent the exact number or layout of physical allocations.

Sliding and global retention differ. Eligible Gemma Metal routes use a bounded sliding ring alongside full-history global storage. The general layer-packed pool keeps full history for mixed attention models so global layers retain their context. Eviction in this drawing illustrates the split retention policy.

06The MoE cousin: Gemma4 26B-A4B

To be clear: Gemma4 E4B is dense — every FFN runs for every token. But the same runtime serves Gemma-4's 26B-A4B mixture-of-experts variant, and its machinery leaks useful ideas back into the dense path.

The qualified A4B architecture has 30 layers, hidden size 2816, and 128 routed experts per layer. Its router selects the top 8 for each token. A shared feed-forward branch also contributes; most routed expert weights are inactive for that token.

Residency depends on the memory budget. The Metal path picks an A4bMappedMoeRoute: a qualified high-memory route keeps mapped expert weights available to the GPU; streamed routes stage selected weights as needed. Apple Silicon uses unified memory, so this is about mapping, residency, and staging, not separate physical CPU and GPU RAM.

metal_compute.zig:51

The planner describes the A4B decode-FFN as an explicit fork/join: shared-expert and routed-expert paths as named resources that join back into the layer output. Today it deliberately stops at planning — a typed description no encoder consumes yet — which is how this codebase grows: the shape first, the lowering when it's earned.

metal_command_planner.zig:854

07From graph to frames

Eligible Metal paths prepare operations and resources for a decode frame. Planning, encoding commands, submitting them, and executing on the GPU are distinct steps.

A decode step starts as a DAG of ops per layer: norm, QKV, rope, attention, projections, the gated FFN. This drawing groups conceptual operations; actual fusion and lowering depend on the route.

Antfly's planner represents eligible work with a FrameDescriptor: an ordered list of PlannedOps grouped into EncoderScopes, with family-specific lowerers for attention setup, gated layers, PLE, and the tail.

metal_command_planner.zig:154 · metal_command_planner.zig:368

Barriers only at real hazards. Within a frame, the runtime tracks read/write byte ranges and emits a Metal buffer barrier only where a genuine RAW/WAR/WAW hazard exists. The old Q8_0 anchor frame still carried 41 encoders and 422 barriers — the ticks here are illustrative hazards, not a GPU capture.

The later performance-plan snapshot recorded 1 compute encoder, 143 planned scopes, planned_barriers = 0 under whole-frame suppression on a serial encoder. The Q8_0 anchor and Q4_0 snapshot are different configurations, not a matched before/after benchmark. Zero explicit barriers does not mean GPU operations run without ordering.

Implementation detail
Conceptual baseline

per-operation dispatch requires coordinating dependencies and lifetimes repeatedly.

Antfly

prepared routes group work and bind resources for each step; encoder policy determines ordering.

metal_runtime.zig:17218

And then the frames overlap. Because the sampled token id stays device-resident (chapter 10), frame N+1 can be encoded from a token that doesn't exist yet on the host — the CPU encodes the next frame before waiting on the current one. The submit→wait→encode bubble can shrink. Historical M4 Air probes reported +9–12% on E2B and +5–8% on E4B with matching tokens. This is CPU/GPU overlap, not two dependent tokens executing concurrently.

metal_executor.zig:1860

Default-on is device-qualified; disable flags and route eligibility still apply.

08Kernels are compiled, not written (mostly)

The matvec kernels that move most of the bytes are not hand-typed Metal. They are generated from schedule tables. A dedicated regeneration check detects drift between the tables and checked-in Metal sources.

One schedule table describes every route as format × row_bucket × epilogue plus tuning knobs; one renderer expands each row through a shared MSL skeleton into a checked-in .metal files. The command zig build quant-kernel-codegen -- --check checks regeneration consistency. This describes the static code-generation path; the repository also has an optional runtime kernel-JIT subsystem with separate mode and qualification controls.

quant_kernel_compiler.zig:695 · quant_kernel_metal_renderer.zig:300

Here is a small-batch schedule example: q4_k, the 2–8-row bucket, no epilogue — 128 threads per threadgroup, 16 columns, 2 rows, simdgroup-tiled reduction. When a sweep finds a better configuration, the fix is an edit to this row and a regenerate, and the diff shows exactly what changed in the emitted Metal. The single-token LM-head MMV in the next chapter is a different route; this 2–8-row schedule is not its launch configuration.

The generated inventory contains 417 extracted Metal entry points. This source census includes generated and hand-written kernels across inference, training, and supporting operations; it is not the dispatch count for one model.

09The LM head problem (a worked example)

The vocabulary projection is large enough to be a useful case study in bandwidth, quantization error, and the difference between an experiment and a default.

Every decode step ends by multiplying the hidden state against all 262,144 vocabulary rows — a [2560 × 262144] matvec. On E4B that segment is about 550 MB of q6_k weights in the recorded artifact, approximately 19.5% of the historical weight-read estimate. That byte calculation does not establish how much latency a different kernel would save.

An opt-in greedy optimization: keep the original Q6_K head and create a q4_k copy in a streaming load-time pass. The tuned termite_q4_k_linear_1x_reduce_v2 MMV nominates candidates;termite_lm_head_q6_k_rescore_top8 rescores them with original weights. Full-logit and sampling callers retain Q6_K. The extra copy uses more resident memory, so TERMITE_METAL_ENABLE_LM_HEAD_Q4_REPACK=q4_k remains opt-in. Historical Air probes improved about 4–5% with matching greedy tokens; candidate truncation is not a proof of equivalence for every prompt.

metal_runtime.zig:9779

The branch that didn't: a q4_0 head looked like free bytes and collapsed generation to an instant end-of-turn token. Measured, struck through, and kept — the ghost path is part of the engineering record, not an embarrassment to hide.

10Device-resident sampling, when eligible

A supported resident route can select a token without copying the full vocabulary logits to the CPU. The canonical host sampler remains available for unsupported cases.

Greedy selection reduces logits to an argmax. Temperature sampling can usetermite_sample_gumbel_partials followed by a reduction that writes a token id to a device buffer. Bounded top-k/top-p routes have their own eligibility checks. The Q4_K head's top-8 Q6_K rescore is a separate greedy optimization, not a universal stage before Gumbel sampling.

metal_kernels.m:8317

Implementation detail
Conceptual baseline

host sampling reads logits and applies the canonical request constraints on the CPU.

Antfly

eligible requests select on device; token ids still reach the host for decoding and streaming.

metal_kernels.m:8317

generation.zig:6888 Unsupported settings or grammar constraints can require a host path.

The payoff is bigger than saved copies: because the sampled id lives in a GPU buffer, the next frame's embedding lookup can consume it directly. That device-resident handoff is what makes chapter 7's pipelined decode frame legal — the CPU encodes frame N+1 against a token the host has never seen.

11MTP: a draft model that reads the main model's mind

Gemma-4 ships an official speculative drafter — a 4-layer, hidden-256 stack that does not build an independent target-style KV cache. It borrows the main model's.

The drafter is query-only: it has Q/O projections and MLPs but no K/V projections at all. Its layers cross-attend the main model's KV banks through donor layers — layers 22 and 23 on E4B (zero-based indices, in the shared-type donor mode) — with a projection pair bridging its 256-wide stack to the 2560-wide backbone. A draft model that literally reads the target's working memory.

gemma4_mtp.zig:139 · gemma4_mtp.zig:167

The loop: the drafter proposes k tokens cheaply, then the main model verifies all k positions together on eligible verifier routes. Accepted tokens amortize a target pass; a mismatch truncates the tail and requires replacement and KV-state handling. Greedy verification aims to preserve the target token sequence. Drafting, verification, and rejected work all cost time, and batched numerical behavior still needs parity checks.

Acceptance alone is not speedup. An earlier E2B Metal CLI pilot recorded 75.9 tok/s target-only versus 63.7 with the BF16 draft at 64% acceptance. Its output did not record a binary identity, so the performance plan labels this directional evidence. Later server probes exercised the slow-path auto-disable and fallback behavior. Metal automatic MTP requires its explicit enable gate; a forced policy is a separate choice. These records do not predict current performance on other devices or runtimes.

12Historical measurements and the bandwidth ceiling

These charts summarize repository benchmark notes, not a new qualification run. An idealized bandwidth ceiling in tokens per second is bandwidth divided by bytes per token; its reciprocal is the lower bound on seconds per token.

The journey. On the fanless M4 Air worktree, E2B went from ~44 tok/s at branch start to 56.5 (about +28% relative to 44): pipelined decode frames, opt-in Q4_K LM-head repack, pair-fusion, PLE Q8_0 staging. The notes also record a sumsq-fusion probe at −12%, measured and struck.

fanless base-M4 Air · 120 GB/s · 16 GB (ceiling ~42 tok/s for E4B)

The initial comparison recorded E4B Q4_0, 64-token circus results on an M4 Pro. Its internal and end-to-end timing boundaries differ, and peer runtime settings were not fully reconciled. Treat these as historical observations; they do not establish a current ranking or prove another runtime omitted model work.
